definition: Microtubules (MTs) are tubulin heterodimers that are arranged in a parallel shape of hollow cylinders which play roles in regulating the mechanical structure and dynamics of cells. Much of the structure and dynamics of MTs is highly ordered. In fact, microtubules were enable to be used as platforms to understand the mechanisms underlying liquidâliquid phase separation, some RNA binding proteins on microtubules leads to the formation of mRNA-rich liquid-like compartments on microtubules.

definition: The processive actin polymerase and bundling protein, VASP, forms liquid-like droplets under physiological conditions in vitro
Condensates promoting actin nucleation

An endocytic patch that consists of an actin-containing structure found at the plasma membrane in cells; formed of networks of branched actin filaments that lie just beneath the plasma membrane and assemble, move, and disassemble rapidly. An example of this is the actin cortical patch found in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

In many of the known yeast cell adhesion proteins, there are amino acid sequences predicted to form amyloid-like β-aggregates. These sequences mediate amyloid formation in vitro. In vivo, these sequences mediate a phase transition from a disordered state to a partially ordered state to create patches of adhesins on the cell surface. These β-aggregated protein patches are called adhesin nanodomains, and their presence greatly increases and strengthens cell-cell interactions in fungal cell aggregation.

Aggresomes are dynamic and reversible structures that form under stressed conditions. Aggresomes are crucial for bacterial fitness, providing a mechanism for spatial and temporal control of protein aggregation.

BAG2 condensates are found in the cytosol and triggered by several forms of stress, particularly hyper-osmotic stress. These condensates facilitate client degradation through the 20S proteasome, independent of ubiquitin. Unlike most condensates, BAG2 condensates do not contain RNA. These structures safeguard cell viability during stress and can move towards the client protein. Inhibition of the proteasome leads to the relocation of BAG2 condensates and autophagy markers to an aggresome-like structure.
Plectin (Plec) via its intrinsically disordered region (IDR)-mediated phase separation promotes osteoblast differentiation by sequestering Anxa2 through phase separation.
In Candida albicans, soluble fragments of Als5p can form amyloid fibers.

Anisosomes are nuclear liquid spherical shells with liquid core formed by demixing of RNA-binding deficient TDP-43  protein molecules. Formation of anisosome droplets represent a liquid crystal formation and is important in age related neurodegenerative diseases.

RNA binding-deficient TDP-43 (produced by neurodegeneration-causing mutations or posttranslational acetylation in its RNA recognition motifs) drove TDP-43 demixing into intranuclear liquid spherical shells with liquid cores. These droplets, which we named "anisosomes", have shells that exhibit birefringence, thus indicating liquid crystal formation.

The ankle link complex (ALC) condensate is a liquid-liquid phase-separated (LLPS) structure at cochlear hair cell stereocilia ankles. It promotes the assembly of the USH2 complex, important for stereocilia integrity and function.

These condensates are located at the tip of the tallest stereocilia within mechanosensory hair cells. Their existence significantly enhances the capacity for actin bundling in these specialized projections, suggesting a potential connection to the determination of the tallest stereocilia
A stable protein complex that contains two actin-related proteins, Arp2 and Arp3, and five novel proteins (ARPC1-5), and functions in the nucleation of branched actin filaments.
Cytoplasmic condensates composed of ribosome‐nascent protein chain complexes
The ABC transporter (Rv1747) has a regulatory cytoplasmic module which undergoes phase separation and forms liquid- like condensates.

RNase Y assembles dynamically into foci in absence of its RNA substrates. This different from similar, bacterial RNase E-based BR bodies, involved in active RNA decay.
Germ plasm in developing oocytes of vertebrates is localized into a special membrane-less structure called Balbiani body (Bb).  Bb is packed with RNAs, mitochondria, Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum.
MARDO (Mitochondria-Associated Ribonucleoprotein DOmain) is a mitochondria-associated condensate that is described to store maternal mRNAs in the oocyte

Germ plasm in developing oocytes of vertebrates is localized into a special membrane-less structure called Balbiani body (Bb).  Bb is packed with RNAs, mitochondria, Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum. Bb in Xenopus is termed mitochondrial cloud .

The Balbiani body is a structure conserved from insects to humans that appears as a large granule, similar to a mRNP granule composed of mRNA and proteins. It has amyloid-like properties and can connect cortical actin. In addition, Wilsch-Bräuninger et al. suggest that the sponge bodies, a subcellular structure in nurse cells and oocytes, are homologous to the mitochondrial cloud in Xenopus oocytes.

Early oocytes of almost all studied animal species contain transient organelle assemblage called the Balbiani body (Bb) or “mitochondrial cloud”[1]. Bb in various species became extremely confusing and the name Balbiani body has been substituted with terms such as yolk nucleus/body/complex, vitelline/nucleus/body, mitochondrial cloud/mass/aggregate, sponge body or even, erroneously, has been equated to the germ plasm. The structure and composition of the Bb differ between species, it is highly dynamic during oocyte growth and in many instances its function(s) remains either highly hypothetical or completely unknown[2]. Bb always contains two essential elements: numerous tightly clustered mitochondria and accumulations of electron-dense granulo-fibrillar material, known as the nuage[1].
A prominent mass in the cytoplasm of previtellogenic oocytes. The cloud contains both mitochondria and electron-dense granulofibrillar material (GFM) and is the source of germinal granule material.

-BAZ2A bodies form in the nucleus and their presence is enhanced by increased concentrations of crowding agents (i.e. PEG8000) and their frequency and size is reduced with increased 16-hexanediol concentration.

Cajal bodies are nuclear bodies which are composed of the scaffolding protein  Coilin and high concentrations of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) which are involved in pre-mRNA splicing.These condensates are also suggested to contribute to RNA metabolism including snRNP biogenesis and telomerase biogenesis.
Cajal

Cajal body (CB) contributes to the biogenesis of small nuclear RNPs (snRNPs), which are involved in pre-mRNA splicing. In addition to snRNPs, CBs also contain another type of RNP: small Cajal body-specific RNPs (scaRNPs). The presence of scaRNPs in the CB serves to modify the snRNA component of snRNPs. CBs also take part in the biogenesis of small nucleolar RNPs (snoRNPs). Like scaRNPs, there are 2 classes of snoRNPs: box H/ACA and box C/D. CBs also contain the RNP responsible for the formation of telomeres, telomerase. Along with snRNPs, scaRNPs and telomerase, the CB is enriched for many proteins[1]. Neuronal CBs concentrate coilin, fibrillarin, SMN (survival of motor neuron) and components of the splicing machinery indicating that they are canonical CBs potentially engaged in the assembly and maturation of spliceosomal snRNPs[2]. Fam118B was identified in a screen for coilin interacting proteins[1]. WRAP53β plays a central role in the maintenance of the nuclear organelles known as Cajal bodies, recruiting factors such as the SMN protein, scaRNAs and telomerase to these bodies[3]. Recent work has found that CB association with certain gene loci contributes to genome organization, especially of chromosome 1, and CBs impact the expression of many genes and RNA splicing. Since the CB plays an important role in the biogenesis of snRNP, scaRNP, snoRNP and telomerase, all of which are required for efficient and rapid cell proliferation, identification of signaling pathways that could be inhibited should be of therapeutic value in the treatment of cancer[1].
Carboxysome is a bacterial organelle that has properties of a biomolecular condensate. Rubisco condensates formation is proposed to optimize the process of photosynthetic carbon fixation.

The shell protein PduBB0 interacts with the enzyme diol-dehy- dratase PduCDE and co-assemble into phase separated liquid droplets. The co-assembly of PduCDE and PduBB0 results in the enhancement of catalytic activity of the enzyme

Carboxysomes in cyanobacteria enclose the enzymes Rubisco and carbonic anhydrase to optimize photosynthetic carbon fixation. Understanding carboxysome assembly has implications in agricultural biotechnology. Here we analyzed the role of the scaffolding protein CcmM of the β-cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942 in sequestrating the hexadecameric Rubisco and the tetrameric carbonic anhydrase, CcaA. We find that the trimeric CcmM, consisting of γCAL oligomerization domains and linked small subunit-like (SSUL) modules, plays a central role in mediation of pre-carboxysome condensate formation through multivalent, cooperative interactions.

Cetrosomes are the main microtubule organising centers (MTOC) of animal cells and thus are critical in regulating cell-cycle progression. Centrosomes nucleate microtubules during mitosis, allowing for chromosomal segregation. Each centrosome contains 2 centrioles arranged perpendicularly and surrounded by pericentriolar material (PCM).

Centrosomes nucleate microtubules during mitosis, allowing for chromosomal segregation. Each centrosome contains 2 centrioles arranged perpendicularly and surrounded by pericentriolar material (PCM).

The Pericentriolar material or cen mRNA granule is a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) condensate that localizes to the Pericentriolar Material (PCM) of the Drosophila centrosome. This condensate acts as a platform for the local translation of Cen,  which is improtant for organizing the mitotic spindle and facilitating mitosis.

Centrosomes are the main microtubule organising centers (MTOC) of animal cells and thus are critical in regulating cell-cycle progression. Centrosomes nucleate microtubules during mitosis, allowing for chromosomal segregation. Each centrosome contains 2 centrioles arranged perpendicularly and surrounded by pericentriolar material (PCM).

A centrosome is a composite material comprising a pair of 200-nm-long barrel-shaped centrioles surrounded by a dynamic protein mass called the pericentriolar material (PCM), which organizes hundreds to thousands of microtubules that build and position the mitotic spindle in metazoans. The seemingly unstructured mitotic PCM provides most of the mass and microtubule nucleation capacity of the centrosome, Mitotic PCM could also be liquid like, the mitotic PCM first assembles through phase separation of SPD-5 molecules around the centrioles. Liquid–liquid phase separation of the SPD-5 scaffold followed by maturation into a gel could explain why mitotic PCM is both spherical and stable.

Pericentriolar matrix, also known as pericentriolar material. A centrosome consists of two barrel-shaped centrioles embedded in a matrix of proteins known as the pericentriolar material (PCM). The PCM serves as a platform for protein complexes that regulate organelle trafficking, protein degradation and spindle assembly. However, unlike other organelles, the PCM is not membrane bound, but rather a dynamic collection of protein complexes and nucleic acids that constitute the organelle's interior and determine its boundary. DYRK3 acts as a central dissolvase of several types of membraneless organelle during mitosis, through its ability to control the condensation of multiple compartments, DYRK3 may link structural and functional roles for RNA, transcription and splicing to the assembly of the mitotic spindle, and be involved in the maintenance of the pericentriolar matrix.

A centrosome is a composite material comprising a pair of 200-nm-long barrel-shaped centrioles surrounded by a dynamic protein mass called the pericentriolar material (PCM), which organizes hundreds to thousands of microtubules that build and position the mitotic spindle in metazoans (1). The seemingly unstructured mitotic PCM provides most of the mass and microtubule nucleation capacity of the centrosome, Mitotic PCM could also be liquid like, the mitotic PCM first assembles through phase separation of SPD-5 molecules around the centrioles. Liquid–liquid phase separation of the SPD-5 scaffold followed by maturation into a gel could explain why mitotic PCM is both spherical and stable

Pericentriolar matrix, also known as pericentriolar material. A centrosome consists of two barrel-shaped centrioles embedded in a matrix of proteins known as the pericentriolar material (PCM). The PCM serves as a platform for protein complexes that regulate organelle trafficking, protein degradation and spindle assembly. Perhaps most important for cell division, the PCM concentrates tubulin and serves as the primary organizing centre for microtubules in metazoan somatic cells. However, unlike other organelles, the PCM is not membrane bound, but rather a dynamic collection of protein complexes and nucleic acids that constitute the organelle's interior and determine its boundary.
A network of small fibers that surrounds the centrioles in cells; contains the microtubule nucleating activity of the centrosome.

The cytosolic DNA sensor cGMP-AMP (cGAMP) synthase (cGAS) detects both pathogenic and mislocalized DNA in the cytoplasm and activates innate immunity. The immunological response to cancer and pathogen infection is dependent on cGAS detection of cytosolic DNA. The spatial limitation of the DNA sensor cGAS prevents abnormal intracellular detection of self-DNA. The development of cytoplasmic foci containing cGAS and DNA is triggered by DNA emerging in the cytoplasm. Human cGAS (h-cGAS) constitutes an important therapeutic target for modulation of antiinflammatory responses that can contribute to the emergence of autoimmune disorders.

DNA binding to cGAS robustly induced the formation of liquid-like droplets in which cGAS was activated. The disordered and positively charged cGAS N terminus enhanced cGAS-DNA phase separation by increasing the valencies of DNA binding. Long DNA was more efficient in promoting cGAS liquid phase separation and cGAS enzyme activity than short DNA. Moreover, free zinc ions enhanced cGAS enzyme activity both in vitro and in cells by promoting cGAS-DNA phase separation. cGAS-DNA phase separation is required to resist negative regulation and allow efficient sensing of immunostimulatory DNA. DNA-induced phase transition of cGAS promotes cGAMP production and innate immune signaling.

Chlamydomonas reinhardtii

Chloroplast stress granules in the eukaryotic green alga assemble upon stress-induced disassembly of the Rubisco holoenzyme in the pyrenoid. This activates the RNA-binding activity of LSU (large Rubisco subunit, P00877), followed by its concurrent aggregation and binding to mRNAs that are released from polysomes.

Chromatin is a complex of DNA and histone proteins that regulates gene expression as well as packaging genetic material to fit inside the cell. The proper functioning of chromatin also necessitates a web of interactions between molecular complexes that alter chromatin shape and organization to change DNA accessibility to transcription factors, resulting in the activation or repression of target DNA locus. Chromatin is divided into three types based on its shape and compaction state: euchromatin, heterochromatin, and centromeric chromatin. Euchromatin is characterized by active genes, broader spacing between nucleosomes, greater accessibility to transcription machinery, and histone modifications and variations that favor active transcription.

Chromatin is partitioned on multiple length scales into subcompartments that differ from each other with respect to their molecular composition and biological function. two different mechanisms for the formation of phase-separated chromatin subcompartments have been proposed. One is based on bridging proteins that cross-link polymer segments with particular properties. Bridging can induce a collapse of the nucleosome chain and associated factors into an ordered globular phase. The other mechanism is based on multivalent interactions among soluble molecules that bind to chromatin. These interactions can induce liquid-liquid phase separation, which drives the assembly of liquid-like nuclear bodies around the respective binding sites on chromatin. Both phase separation mechanisms can explain that chromatin bodies are dynamic spherical structures, which can coalesce and are in constant and rapid exchange with the surrounding nucleoplasm.
A dispersed and relatively uncompacted form of chromatin that is in a transcription-competent conformation.

Chromogranin condensates are liquid-like assemblies forming in the lumen of the Trans Golgi Network.  The mildly acidic environment inside the Golgi lumen promotes the formation of these condensates and recruits the clients proteins like proinsulin. The formation of liquid-like assemblies provides a mechanism for a receptor-independent sorting of cargo molecules.

Large dense-core vesicles (LDCVs) are large vesicles filled with multiple neuropeptides, hormones, and neurotransmitters that participate in various physiological processes. The formation of these vesicles is sensitive to pH and Ca2+ concentration

Cleavage bodies are nuclear bodies which contain factors that are necessary for RNA transcription and/or processing. Cleavage bodies often colocalize with other nuclear bodies, such as DDX1 body and Cajal body

Cleavage bodies is a kind of nuclear PMLO (proteinaceous membrane-less organelles) located in Nucleus, It contains no DNA or RNA and it is fluid shaped as a spherical, it is associated with RNA metabolism, potentially serves as storage/assembly sites for proteins involved in transcription, splicing 3â-end processing of pre-mRNAs, and RNA degradation. They are formed as a result of highly regulated and reversible liquid-liquid demixing phase separation and represent condensed liquid droplets, which are invariantly enriched in intrinsically disordered proteins.

The conjusome plays an important role in the conjugation events that occur in Tetrahymena thermophila. The conjusome appears in the anterior of conjugant pairs during the early stages of new macronuclei (anlagen) development. It lacks a membrane, and is composed of a network of fibrous, electron dense material, containing background cytoplasm and ribosomes. Several proteins localize to this organelle, including Pdd1p, a chromodomain protein that participates in the formation of chromatin-containing structures in developing macronuclear anlagen

An extracellular matrix consisting mainly of proteins (especially collagen) and glycosaminoglycans (mostly as proteoglycans) that provides not only essential physical scaffolding for the cellular constituents but can also initiate crucial biochemical and biomechanical cues required for tissue morphogenesis, differentiation and homeostasis. The components are secreted by cells in the vicinity and form a sheet underlying or overlying cells such as endothelial and epithelial cells.

As the final stage of cell cycle, actin filaments, myosin-II (Myo2), and numerous other proteins form a cytokinetic contractile ring that invaginates the plasma membrane to form a furrow that cleaves the cell into two daughter cells, this process is known as cytokinesis. Anillins are scaffold proteins of cytokinesis organizing center and their impairment impairs cytokinesis in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, resulted from aberrant contractile rings.

A cytoskeletal structure composed of filamentous protein that forms beneath the membrane of many cells or organelles, in the plane of cell or organelle division. Ring contraction is associated with centripetal growth of the membrane that divides the cytoplasm of the two daughter cells or organelles.
Any microtubule in the cytoplasm of a cell.

CBs is a collective term used for biomolecular condensates with members of ubiquitin ligases components. CBs are speculated function as aggresome precursors or storage compartments that segregate potentially harmful excess ubiquitin ligases molecules from the cytosol dilute phase.

The condensate forms from Cpeb1b, Pabpc1b, Tent2, and shha mRNA in zebrafish, exhibiting liquid-like properties. It is necessary for cytoplasmic polyadenylation of shha mRNA, promoting Hedgehog signaling and supporting hematopoiesis during zebrafish embryogenesis.

The intrinsically disordered regions in the N-terminal domain of the unphosphorylated CPEB4 phase separate into inactive, liquid-like droplets, CPEB4 granules. This process is coordinated by Cdk1 through inactivating CPEB1 while activating CPEB4, controlling the dynamic and reversible regulation of CPEB4 with that of CPEB1, integrating phase-specific signal transduction pathways to control cell cycle progression.
Phase separated cytoplasmic proteins forming aggregates in the cytoplasm. A hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases is the accumulation of cytoplasmic protein aggregates in neurons.

Ddx3xb condensates are ATP- and IDR-dependent assemblies identified in developing zebrafish embryos. The maintenance of liquid-like properties has been shown to facilitate mRNA translation during Maternal-to-zygotic (MZT) in early embryos.

FXR1 undergoes phase separation to form mRNP granules in Late Spermatids (LS) and are indispensable for the male fertility in mice. FXR1 recruits translation factors like ELF4G3 into the condensates. The fusion of these FXR1 condensates with RNP granules in germ cells activate the translation of the stored mRNA .
With MEX3B identified as a constituent of P-bodies, additional non-colocalizing condensates composed of labeled MEX3B are observed in MCF7 cells.

RNP granules are membrane-less organelles composed of RNA and proteins. RNA-binding proteins are key components of RNP granules. RNP granules deliver localized mRNAs delivered to areas of local protein synthesis.
In yeast, translational condensates are specialized, membraneless compartments that form in response to cellular stress
WHI3 undergoes phase separation to form droplets with different biophysical properties. The properties of WHI3 droplets and their phase separation depends on different RNAs which interact with WHI3.
A ribonucleoprotein granule located in the cytoplasm.
Condensation of DIAPH3 proteins upon cellular stress, named as "D-granule

DDX1 body is a type of nuclear bodies. DDX1 bodies contain the protein DEAD box DDX1 protein, which  is a potential RNA unwinding protein linked to RNA processing and transport. Cleavage bodies and DDX1 bodies are frequently found colocalizing in the nucleus.

Eukaryotic cells are inhomogeneously crowded with biological macromolecules (proteins and nucleic acids) and often contain numerous cellular bodies, including proteinaceous membrane-less organelles (PMLOs), They are formed as a result of highly regulated and reversible liquid-liquid demixing phase separation and represent condensed liquid droplets, which are invariantly enriched in intrinsically disordered proteins, DDX1 bodies is a kind of these bodies located in nucleus, It is fluid and related to the pre-mRNA processing.

Membrane-associated RNP assembly in Escherichia coli, involved in ribosomal RNA (rRNA) processing and mRNA degradation. Composed of three central components: RNA helicase B, RNase E and Polynucleotide phosphorylase (PNPase). Activity regulated by bacterial, regulatory small RNAs (sRNA). Synonymous with 'BR-bodies' described in other bacterial species. Evidence for most components listed as members is co-purification with RNase E.

53BP1 Mitotic Stress Bodies (MSBs) are phase-separated condensates formed during mitotic stress in human cancer cells, primarily near centromeres. MSBs are driven by p53, are associated with DNA, and play a role in DNA repair and mitotic stress response.

Double-strand breaks can be caused by a variety of physical and chemical factors, such as ionizing radiation and radiomimetic medicines, but they can also develop as secondary lesions during replication and DNA repair after exposure to a variety of genotoxins. Repair proteins aggregate at damaged areas in response to double strand breaks (DSB), forming membrane-less  subnuclear foci, supporting DNA repair.

A phase-separated biomolecular assembly is established at sites of DNA damage, primarily mediated by poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) and its affinity for double-stranded DNA. The condensate functions to stabilize broken DNA ends, promote the recruitment of repair factors, and is subject to regulation by PARP1-mediated PARylation, which facilitates disassembly following the completion of repair.
The SOSS-INTAC condensate is a nuclear condensate. It regulates R-loop levels and facilitates genome stability. This condensate participates in preventing transcription-replication conflicts

Bacterial single-stranded DNA binding protein (SSB) form condenates that are described to store DNA repair proteins that interact with SSB. It was shoiwn that levated levels of single-stranded DNA during genomic stress might dissolve SSB condensates, enabling rapid mobilization of SSB and SSB-interacting proteins to sites of DNA damage.
TopBP1 condensates are reversible and were shown to fuse. TopBP1 condensation is proposed to act as a molecular switch that amplifies ATR activity.

DNA damage response proteins such as γH2AX, ATM, 53BP1, RAD51, and the MRE11/RAD50/NBS1 complex, that accumulate and/or are modified in the vicinity of a chromosomal DNA double-strand break to form microscopically visible, subnuclear foci called DNA damage foci, also called (ionizing) radiationâinduced foci (IRIF or RIF) or DNA repair foci. The discovery of DNA damage foci has opened a new dimension to the field of DNA damage signaling. Analysis of the spatiotemporal dynamics of DSB induction and repair in situ or even in live cells has now become a standard method in many different fields.

There are a number of different names in use for DNA damage foci, such as (ionizing) radiation-induced foci (IRIF or RIF) or DNA repair foci. In general they all refer to local accumulations or modifications of DNA damage response proteins that form at the sites of DNA double-strand breaks and can be visualized through microscopic imaging following immunocyto- or -histochemical detection or fluorescent protein tagging. The first and most prominent protein for which foci formation at the site of a double strand break was described is the histone variant H2AX which gets phosphorylated at its C-terminal Ser-139 residue by the DNA damage-activated kinases ATM, ATR, and DNA-PK to form γH2AX. γH2AX then acts as a docking station for other DNA damage signaling factors such as MDC1 and 53BP1 which accumulate to form foci in a histone-modification-dependent manner[1]. IRIF are dynamic structures containing thousands of copies of proteins involved in various aspects of DSB repair and signaling. These proteins include phosphorylated ATM, 53BP1, MDC1, RAD51, MRN complex (MRE11/RAD50/NBS1), RNF8/KIAA0646, RNF168, and BRCA1-A complex (BRCA1, BARD1, UIMC1/RAP80, FAM175A/Abraxas, BRCC3/BRCC36, BRE/BRCC45 and MERIT40/NBA1)[2].

Dps (DNA-binding protein from starved cells) is the most abundant protein component of the nucleoid formaing condensates. Dps compacts DNA into a dense complex and protects it from damage and acts as a regulator of transcription.
Monomers in elastin can phase separate and self-assemble into polymer networks with elasticity and robustness.

EndoLysosomal Cesicular Assemblies (ELVAs) are large, protein-rich compartments found in mouse oocytes. They sequester aggregated proteins and are characterized by the presence of lysosomal and autophagic markers. ELVAs are driven by the protein RUFY1, which forms a structural matrix within these assemblies.
Ede1 is an endocytic  protein. Excess Ede1 in yeast cells phase separates into large condensates which  are able recruit other endocytic proteins.

Endocytic condensates are membraneless compartments formed by endocytic coat proteins containing prion-like domains. These condensates assemble at the plasma membrane to organize proteins, which helps drive membrane invagination for cellular uptake through endocytosis.

A protein-DNA complex formed by the association of a distinct set of general and specific transcription factors with a region of enhancer DNA. The cooperative assembly of an enhanceosome confers specificity of transcriptional regulation.

Enhancers are key regulatory elements that govern gene expression programs in response to developmental signals. TGF β pathway drives the assembly of an enhancer-cluster and precise gene activation. TGF β pathway coactivator JMJD3 is essential to maintain these structures.
MegaTrans components (ESR1 and GATA3) are shown to phase separate and form micro-sized condensates in the presence of  5% polyethylene glycol asa crowding agent.

In human breast cancer cells, the acute 17β-estradiol-dependent activation of functional enhancers requires assembly of an enhancer RNA-dependent ribonucleoprotein (eRNP) complex exhibiting properties of phase-separated condensates. While acute ligand-dependent assembly of eRNPs resulted in enhancer activation sensitive to chemical disruption of phase separation, chronically activated enhancers proved resistant to such disruption, with progressive maturation of eRNPs to a more gel-like state. Acute, but not chronic, stimulation resulted in ligand-induced, condensin-dependent changes in spatial chromatin conformation based on homotypic enhancer association, resulting in cooperative enhancer-activation events.

source_name: nuclear bodies that occur at super enhancers in mESCs

definition: ERESs (endoplasmic reticulum (ER) exit sites) are dynamic, liquid-like condensates formed by the phase separation of SEC16A and other early secretory pathway proteins. These condensates are described to be sensitive to the concentration of the kinase DYRK3. The SEC16A protein, particularly its intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), plays a role in driving the liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) that forms these condensates

ESCRT condensate  in yeast refers to the biomelcular condensate  formed by the early components of the Endosomal Sorting Complex Required for Transport (ESCRT) machinery at the membrane of the yeast lysosome or endosomes
cell-membrane associated condensate driven by SDC4 critical for exosome formation and secretion
A structure lying external to one or more cells, which provides structural support, biochemical or biomechanical cues for cells or tissues.

Ferritin–NCOA4 condensate formation is driven by NCOA4 self-interaction and responsible for ferritin degradation. These condesates are common substrates for macroautophagy and endosomal microautophagy.
FRQ phase separates in a temperature-dependent manner, altering its phosphorylation by CK1.

When encapsulated in artificial cell-like systems created by microfluidics and under specific circumstances, such as being in a GDP-bound state and on conditions simulating the crowded environment of the cytoplasm that promote its oligomerization, bacterial FtsZ can undergo phase separation and form condensates.
FtsZ/SlmA  body is a bacterial nucleoprotein complex condensate which forms upon the interaction of FtsZ with SlmA. This condensate is dynamic and has liquid-liquid phase separation features.

source_name: Ftsz-rich droplets at specific chromosomal DNA sites

definition: The N-terminal domain of Galectin-3 contains aromatic residues which interact to phase separate the domain. This process is important for the extracellular agglutination function of Galectin-3.
A homodimeric protein complex that is capable of binding a range of carbohydrates and is involved in anti-inflammatory and pro-apoptotic processes.
Nuclear bodies are membraneless, RNA-rich organelles in the cell nucleus that concentrate certain nuclear proteins and RNA-protein complexes.

Eukaryotic cells are inhomogeneously crowded with biological macromolecules (proteins and nucleic acids) and often contain numerous cellular bodies, including proteinaceous membrane-less organelles (PMLOs), They are formed as a result of highly regulated and reversible liquid-liquid demixing phase separation and represent condensed liquid droplets, which are invariantly enriched in intrinsically disordered proteins. Gemini of Cajal bodies, also called as Gemini of coiled bodies or nuclear gems, is a kind of these bodies located in Nucleus of spherical shape, It do not contain snRNPs. The function of nuclear gems is still unknown, may be related to further maturation, storage or recycling of splicing factors.

Nuclear gems are enigmatic structures of unknown function. Until recently, the only components localized in gems were members of the SMN complex—the SMN protein and Gemins. In the cytoplasm, the SMN complex is essential for snRNP biogenesis but its role in the nucleus is unclear [29]. Loss of SMN protein results in degeneration of motor neurons and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). An accompanying feature of SMA is loss of gems, which are also disrupted in the motor neuron disease—amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

Founder granules are ribonucleoprotein (RNP) condensates formed by the agglomeration of oskar (osk) mRNA RNPs during late oogenesis in Drosophila. These granules are enriched at the posterior of the oocyte and are distinct from germ granules, they are transient and not inherited during embryogenesis. They serve to localize osk mRNA (as well as CycB and nos mRNA and others).

Germ plasm, a specialized cytoplasm present at the posterior of the early Drosophila embryo, is necessary and sufficient for germ cell formation. Germ plasm is rich in mitochondria and contains electron dense structures called polar granules, which are necessary for germ line formation and might be related to P bodies. In zebra-fish, germ plasm are proved to be related phase-separated structures. Throughout development, many germ cell-specific mRNAs and proteins condense as a single large aggregate (Bb), which disperse throughout oogenesis and upon fertilization accumulates again into relatively large assemblies (Gp). In many organisms, germ cell fate is imposed on cells through the cytoplasmic inheritance of germ plasm (Gp).

In many organisms, germ cell fate is imposed on cells through the cytoplasmic inheritance of P granule-like structures, called germ plasm (Gp). In zebrafish, Gp originates from an evolutionary conserved electron-dense aggregate in the oocyte, called the Balbiani body (Bb).
Differentiated cytoplasm associated with a pole of an oocyte, egg or early embryo that will be inherited by the cells that will give rise to the germ line.

G-bodies are cytoplasmic granules which form in yeast from the aggregation of glycolysis enzymes in response to hypoxic stress. The formation of G-bodies is linked to a higher consumption rate of glucose and increased cell survival.
PFK-1.1 condensates in Caenorhabditis elegans do not correspond to stress granules and might represent novel metabolic subcompartments

In hypoxic stress conditions, glycolysis enzymes assemble into singular cytoplasmic granules called glycolytic (G) bodies. G body formation in yeast correlates with increased glucose consumption and cell survival. Glycolysis enzymes are non-canonical RNA binding proteins, sharing many common mRNA substrates that are also integral constituents of G bodies. Targeting nonspecific endoribonucleases to G bodies reveals that RNA nucleates G body formation and maintains its structural integrity. Consistent with a phase separation mechanism of biogenesis, recruitment of glycolysis enzymes to G bodies relies on multivalent homotypic and heterotypic interactions. G bodies fuse in vivo and are largely insensitive to 1,6-hexanediol, consistent with a hydrogel-like composition.
The protein GM130 (GOGA2) forms a membrane-bound RNA-dependent condensate that keeps the integrity of the Golgi ribbon.

Biomolecular condensates are micron-scale compartments in eukaryotic cells that operate to concentrate proteins and nucleic acids but lack surrounding membranes. RNA metabolism, ribosome biogenesis, the DNA damage response, and signal transmission are all affected by these condensates. Recent research has discovered that multivalent macromolecular interactions promote liquid-liquid phase separation, which is a fundamental organizing principle for biomolecular condensates.

The Golgi is surrounded by a ribosome-excluding matrix. The cis-Golgi-localized golgin GM130 can phase-separate to form dynamic, liquid-like condensates in vitro and in vivo. The overexpression of each of the remaining cis (golgin160, GMAP210)- and trans (golgin97, golgin245, GCC88, GCC185)-golgins results in novel protein condensates. Pairs of golgins overexpressed in the same cell form distinct juxtaposed condensates. In addition to their established roles as vesicle tethers, phase separation may be a common feature of the golgin family that contributes to Golgi organization.

Chromatin is a complex of DNA and histone proteins that regulates gene expression as well as packaging genetic material to fit inside the cell. The proper functioning of chromatin also necessitates a web of interactions between molecular complexes that alter chromatin shape and organization to change DNA accessibility to transcription factors, resulting in the activation or repression of target DNA locus. Chromatin is divided into three types based on its shape and compaction state: euchromatin, heterochromatin, and centromeric chromatin. Heterochromatin is related with gene silencing and is characterized by being less accessible than euchromatin and transcriptionally less active. In the nucleus, heterochromatin separates from euchromatin and is concentrated in the nuclear periphery and regions around the nucleolus.

The sex body is a nuclear condensate formed during male meiosis in mouse pachytene spermatocytes, driven by the phase-separating protein MAPS. It is involved in silencing unsynapsed sex chromosomes and regulating chromatin behaviors.

In both Drosophila and mammalian cells, heterochromatin domains exhibit dynamics that are characteristic of liquid phase-separation, including sensitivity to the disruption of weak hydrophobic interactions, and reduced diffusion, increased coordinated movement and inert probe exclusion at the domain boundary. Known components of heterochromatin such as nucleosomes and DNA preferentially partition into the HP1α droplets, but molecules such as the transcription factor TFIIB show no preference. Both unmodified and phosphorylated HP1α induce rapid compaction of DNA strands into puncta, although with different characteristics.
A compact and highly condensed form of chromatin that is refractory to transcription.

The Hippo signalosome condensates are formed by LATS2 and its associated proteins in response to cytoskeletal reorganization. These dynamic condensates play a role in spatially organizing and regulating Hippo pathway signaling.

TAZ condensates are dynamic and are primarily formed through the involvement of the protein TAZ. Their formation is modulated by RNA-binding protein FUS, which acts as a dissolver of the condensates. Transcriptional co-activators are recruited into the condensates, such as  TEAD4, BRD4, and CycT1.

The Histone Locus Body (HLB) is a nucleus subdomain characterized by the concentration of components required for histone gene transcription and pre-mRNA processing. Histone mRNAs production takes place in HLBs.

The histone locus body (HLB) contains factors required for processing histone pre-mRNAs, which is present throughout the interphase of the cell cycle, but disappear during mitosis. It is associated with the genes that code for histones, suggesting that it may function to concentrate processing factors at their site of action. Besides, as one of the coilin-containing bodies like Cajal bodies , HLB in nuclei of late two-cell embryos are heterogeneous in both morphology and molecular composition, but their heterogeneity is not related to the number of coilin-positive intranuclear HLB structures.

The histone locus body (HLB) contains factors required for processing histone pre-mRNAs[1]. Production of histone mRNAs occurs in HLB, a subdomain of the nucleus defined by a concentration of factors necessary for histone gene transcription and pre-mRNA processing. HLB formation involves a combination of ordered and stochastic assembly steps, and cell cycle regulated changes in the HLB occur to activate histone gene expression during S phase[2].

Hypersomatic shock foci are novel protein aggregates that are found to form instantly in response to hypersomatic stress. These foci appear/disappear seconds after shock onset/removal, corresponding to changes in cell volume.

Proteins can aggregate in response to stresses, including hyperosmotic shock. Formation and disassembly of aggregates is a relatively slow process. We describe a novel instant response of the cell to hyperosmosis, during which chaperones and other proteins form numerous foci with properties uncharacteristic of classical aggregates. These foci appeared/disappeared seconds after shock onset/removal, in close correlation with cell volume changes.

IL-1β-Induced INAVA Condensates are a specific physiological manifestation of INAVA condensates formed in response to the inflammatory cytokine Interleukin-1β (IL-1β). They represent a rapid physiological inflammatory response that naturally resolves within a few hours through disassembly rather than protein degradation

INAVA condensates are membraneless compartments formed via phase separation in response to cellular stressors-such as reactive oxygen species or proteasome inhibitors-to regulate protein ubiquitination and degradation.

Inclusion bodies are insoluble aggregates of misfolded proteins inside the cell. A common pathogenic event in a range of neurodegenerative illnesses is aggregated proteins from the cytoplasm of nerve cells and glia. Misfolding and aggregation of huntingtin (Htt) protein results in Huntington's disease (HD), which is the most prevalent inherited neurodegenerative disease. The HD mutation causes an excessively long polyglutamine (polyQ) expansion in the Htt, which makes the protein more prone to aggregate.

Inclusion bodies are insoluble aggregates of misfolded proteins inside the cell. A common pathogenic event in a range of neurodegenerative illnesses is aggregated proteins from the cytoplasm of nerve cells and glia.

Inclusion Body-Associated Granules (IBAGs) are defined as dynamic substructures within viral inclusion bodies (IBs). IBAGs are functionally specialized for translation-related processes, distinct from the replication-focused IBs
Cauliflower Mosaic Virus  forms inclusion bodies during infection, which are mostly made of the viral protein P6 and are the sites of viral activity.

TDP‐25 inclusions are studied in neurons and show amorphous morphology and gel‐like biophysical properties. Aggregation‐prone TDP‐25 fragment (residues 220‐414 of full‐length human TDP‐43) is known to be implicated in ALS/FTD pathogenesis.

Huntingtin exon1 proteins can form reversible liquid-like assemblies, a process driven by huntingtin's polyQ tract and proline-rich region. In cells and in vitro, the liquid-like assemblies converted to solid-like assemblies with a fibrillar structure. Mutant huntingtin protein (mHtt) is unstable and accumulates in large intracellular inclusions both in affected individuals and when expressed in eukaryotic cells. mHtt inclusions are dynamic, mobile, gel-like structures that concentrate mHtt together with the disaggregase Hsp104.

Studies with non-segmented negative-sense (NNS) RNA viruses have uncovered a key role of LLPS in the formation of viral inclusion bodies (IBs), sites of viral protein concentration in the cytoplasm of infected cells.
A discrete intracellular part formed of aggregated molecules such as proteins or other biopolymers.

Inflammasomes are multiprotein platforms for caspase-1 activation which develop in response to a variety of outside and endogenous danger signals, resulting in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and the stimulation of inflammatory cell death via caspase-1 activation.
TIFA-TRAF6 condensates cluster in a liquid-like state as “microreactors” for recruiting downstream signaling molecules affecting the ALPK1-TIFA-TRAF6 signaling pathway.
Insulator bodies are specific nuclear speckles  that function as regulatory elements in modulating enhancer-promoter interactions. Insulator bodies are enriched in chromatin insulator proteins.

Eukaryotic cells are inhomogeneously crowded with biological macromolecules (proteins and nucleic acids) and often contain numerous cellular bodies, including proteinaceous membrane-less organelles (PMLOs), They are formed as a result of highly regulated and reversible liquid-liquid demixing phase separation and represent condensed liquid droplets, which are invariantly enriched in intrinsically disordered proteins. Insulator bodies is a kind of these bodies located in nucleus without any DNA or RNA components and itâs periphery-associated, proved to be related to the response to osmotic stress. Under the osmotic stress, Chromatin insulators assist in the formation of higher-order chromatin structures by mediating long-range contacts between distant genomic sites, It has been suggested that insulators accomplish this task by forming dense nuclear foci termed insulator bodies that result from the coalescence of multiple protein-bound insulators.

The focal adhesion (FA) condensate is a membrane-less condensate formed by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) at the FA periphery. It is improtant for focal adhesion morphology, cytoskeletal dynamics, and mechanical force sensing.

Integrin adhesion complexes (IACs) are integrin-based plasma-membrane-associated compartments where cells sense environmental cues. The physical mechanisms and molecular interactions that mediate initial IAC formation are unclear. We found that both p130Cas ('Cas') and Focal adhesion kinase ('FAK') undergo liquid-liquid phase separation in vitro under physiologic conditions. Cas- and FAK- driven phase separation is sufficient to reconstitute kindlin-dependent integrin clustering in vitro with recombinant mammalian proteins. In vitro condensates and IACs in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) exhibit similar sensitivities to environmental perturbations including changes in temperature and pH. Furthermore, mutations that inhibit or enhance phase separation in vitro reduce or increase the number of IACs in MEFs, respectively.
Organized structure of distinctive morphology and function, not bounded by a lipid bilayer membrane and occurring within the cell. Includes ribosomes, the cytoskeleton and chromosomes.
L-bodies, or localization bodies, are cytoplasmic RNP granules in Xenopus laevis oocytes, important for embryonic patterning, localizing maternal mRNAs.

In this work, we have identified Xenopus oocyte transport RNPs, here termed localization-bodies (L-bodies), as novel biomolecular condensates. L-bodies are RNP granules composed of a nondynamic mRNA-containing phase enmeshed in a dynamic protein-containing layer. These large condensates contain a heterogeneous population of localized mRNAs, including vg1. Incorporation of mRNAs into L-bodies is correlated with localization and appears to rely on selective enrichment, specified by sequence features of resident mRNAs. Biochemical isolation and proteomic analysis of L-bodies reveals a high degree of compositional similarity to other classes of cytoplasmic RNP granules, with the majority of identified proteins showing either direct conservation with other RNP granule types, or a shared enrichment of multivalent RNA binding domains and IDRs.

The dual specificity tyrosine-phosphorylation-regulated kinase 3 (DYRK3) phase separates and form speckles which are similar to P-granules in C. elegans. In its inactive form, DYRK3 prevents the dissolution of stress granules.
Mast cell extracellular granules (MCEGs) are condensates found in the extracellular space, assembled through electrostatic interactions between glycosaminoglycans and polyamines.

McdB protein Is crucial for organize ng reaction centers of Synechococcus elongatus where carbon dioxide in concerted into sugars. McdB condensates are suggested to enhance this process, as altering McdB affects phase separation properties and results in changes in organization of reaction centers.

Master transcription factors (TFs) and the Mediator coactivator form phase-separated condensates at super-enhancers, which compartmentalize and concentrate the transcription apparatus at key cell identity genes. Hundreds of molecules of Pol II and mediator are concentrated in condensates at super-enhancers and large numbers of splicing factors are concentrated in nuclear speckles, some of which occur at highly active transcription sites.
Phase-separated RNP granule involved in RNA storage, translation, and intercellular communication.

miRISC is a multi-protein assembly that identifies mRNAs targeted for repression using microRNAs (miRNAs). In vitro and in living cells, it is demonstrated that two core protein components of human miRISC, Argonaute2 (Ago2) and TNRC6B, condense into phase-separated droplets.

To exert their regulatory function, miRNAs associate with Argonaute proteins to form the core of the miRNA-induced silencing complex (miRISC). miRISC uses the sequence information in the miRNA as a guide to bind complementary sequences in mRNAs targeted for silencing.

A ribonucleoprotein complex that contains members of the Argonaute family of proteins, small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) or microRNAs (miRNAs), and miRNA or siRNA-complementary mRNAs, in addition to a number of accessory factors. The RISC complex is involved in posttranscriptional repression of gene expression through downregulation of translation or induction of mRNA degradation.

Mitochondria, the only semiautonomous organelles in mammalian cells, possess a circular, double-stranded genome termed mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). While nuclear genomic DNA compaction, chromatin compartmentalization and transcription are known to be regulated by phase separation, how the mitochondrial nucleoid, a highly compacted spherical suborganelle, is assembled and functions is unknown. Here we assembled mitochondrial nucleoids in vitro and show that mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) undergoes phase separation with mtDNA to drive nucleoid self-assembly. Moreover, nucleoid droplet formation promotes recruitment of the transcription machinery via a special, co-phase separation that concentrates transcription initiation, elongation and termination factors, and retains substrates to facilitate mtDNA transcription.

Mitochondrial RNA (mtRNA) granules are RNA-rich granules located in close proximity to nucleoids inside mintochondria. mtRNA granules contain newly transcribed mtRNAS and various proteins participating in post-transcriptional processing and regulation of mtRNA, and mitoribosome assembly.

Eukaryotic cells are inhomogeneously crowded with biological macromolecules (proteins and nucleic acids) and often contain numerous cellular bodies, including proteinaceous membrane-less organelles (PMLOs), They are formed as a result of highly regulated and reversible liquid-liquid demixing phase separation and represent condensed liquid droplets, which are invariantly enriched in intrinsically disordered proteins. Mitochondrial RNA granules is a kind of these bodies of spherical shape that located in mitochondria with mitochondrial mRNAs and mitochondrial ribosomes components and itâs proved to be related to the posttranscriptional RNA processing and biogenesis of mitochondrial ribosomes.

MORC3 forms phase-separated condensates with liquid-like properties in the cell nucleus, called MORC3 nuclear bodies (NBs). Nuclear bodies are membraneless organelles in the cell nucleus that concentrate certain nuclear proteins.

Mutator foci are perinuclear germline foci that connect with nuclear pores and P granules to promote short RNA amplification. Mutator foci are where RRF-1, a RdRP, and other Mutator complex proteins cluster. It is suggested that Mutator foci form as a result of MUT-16's liquid-liquid phase separation and they  have characteristics of phase-separated condensates.

HRDE-2 interacts with SIMR-1, HRDE-2 colocalizes with SIMR-1 at SIMR foci, HRDE-2 interacts with HRDE-1 confirmed by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry, HRDE-2 promotes specificity of HRDE-1 for WAGO-class small RNAs.
MUT-16 foci have many properties consistent with a phase-separated condensate and propose that Mutator foci form through liquid-liquid phase separation of MUT-16.

A type of punctate focus localized to the perinuclear region of germline cytoplasm in C. elegans. Mutator foci are required for RNA interference (RNAi) and serve as sites of small inhibitory RNA (siRNA) amplification. As such, proteins that localize to mutator foci include RNA-directed RNA polymerases (RdRPs) and beta-nucleotidyltransferases. Mutator foci are distinct from, but adjacent to or partially overlap, P granules.

The arsenite-induced necrosome form within stress granules during arsenite-induced necroptosis. Stress granules serve as platforms for necrosome assembly, where ZBP1 recruits RIPK3, leading to the phosphorylation and activation of MLKL. This sequence ultimately leads to necroptosis, a regulated form of cell death. Based on previous research, the necrosome under these conditions is closely associated with oxidative stress and Z-RNA binding by ZBP1.
Negri bodies (NBs) are inclusions or viral factories in the cytoplasm of the host cell where rabies virus replicates.

Replication of Mononegavirales occurs in viral factories which form inclusions in the host-cell cytoplasm. For rabies virus, those inclusions are called Negri bodies (NBs). NB have characteristics similar to those of liquid organelles: they are spherical, they fuse to form larger structures, and they disappear upon hypotonic shock.
A prolongation or process extending from a nerve cell, e.g. an axon or dendrite.

RNP granules are membrane-less organelles composed of RNA and proteins. RNA-binding proteins are key components of RNP granules. RNP granules deliver localized mRNAs delivered to areas of local protein synthesis.

Neuronal RNP granules are nonmembrane bound macromolecular condensates that concentrate certain sets of mRNAs and regulatory proteins, allowing them to travel longer distances to axons or dendrites. RNP granules in neurons have a dual role in regulating the translation of linked mRNAs: at rest, they impede mRNA translation, but once activated, they fuel local protein synthesis.

Neuronal RNP granules are nonmembrane bound macromolecular condensates that concentrate certain sets of mRNAs and regulatory proteins, allowing them to travel longer distances to axons or dendrites. RNP granules in neurons have a dual role in regulating the translation of linked mRNAs: at rest, they impede mRNA translation, but once activated, they fuel local protein synthesis.
Rbfox1 is an low complexity domain containing protein that form liquid droplets and amyloid-like fibers and promiscuously links various nuclear and cytoplasmic RNP granules.

In C. elegans, the TIAR-2/TIA protein inhibits axon regeneration through cell-autonomous action. In vivo, TIAR-2 forms granules and undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation in vitro. Axon damage causes a momentary rise in the quantity of TIAR-2 granules.

Neuronal granules are also referred to as neuronal transport granules, RNA-transporting granules, neuronal RNA granules, dendritic P-body like structures (dlP-bodies), FMRP granules and Staufen granules. They are broadly identified by the presence of two highly conserved proteins: Staufen, a double-stranded RNA-binding protein and FMRP. As a kind of cytoplasmic RNP bodies located in Cytoplasm of neurons, neuronal transport RNPs have highly specialized functions and have been shown to interact or co-localize with components of GW/P bodies, it's microtubule-dependent and contain Silenced mRNAs and ribosomes components. Neuronal RNA bodies is of spherical shape with fluid characteristics, proved to be associated with rotein synthesis in response to exogenous stimuli.

Insulin-like growth factor II mRNA-binding protein (IMP) zip code-binding proteins participate in mRNA localization, and in motile cells IMP-containing granules are dispersed around the nucleus and in cellular protrusions. We isolated the IMP1-containing RNP granules and found that they represent a unique RNP entity distinct from neuronal hStaufen and/or fragile X mental retardation protein granules, processing bodies, and stress granules. Granules were 100-300 nm in diameter and consisted of IMPs, 40 S ribosomal subunits, shuttling heterologous nuclear RNPs, poly(A)-binding proteins, and mRNAs.

In mammalian neurons, mRNAs to be targeted to these distant sites can be packaged into Neuronal granules (NGs), where they can remain translationally repressed until they are released at their final destination and translated in response to specific exogenous stimuli. Like stress granules (SGs), NGs contain mRNA, small and large ribosomal subunits, translation initiation factors and RNA-binding proteins that regulate mRNA function. Despite possessing ribosomes, mRNAs present within NGs are probably not translated until they reach the synapse, where their translation may require activating stimuli. SGs and NGs possess many of the same protein components, and Staufen, for example, can be transferred from NGs to SGs during stress in rat oligodendrocytes.

A ribonucleoprotein complex that is found in the cytoplasm of axons and dendrites, and transports translationally silenced mRNAs to dendritic synapses, where they are released and translated in response to specific exogenous stimuli.

NPR1 contains intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). In response to SA, NPR1 undergoes transition into cytoplasmic condensate-like structures enriched with proteins regulating ETI cell death, DNA damage response, redox metabolism, and ubiquitination. This SA-triggered NPR1 condensation is mediated through conserved cysteine clusters within its IDRs and is required for formation of a functional NPR1-CRL3 adaptor complex in the cytoplasm. Using cell biology, molecular, and genetic analyses, we demonstrate that recruitment of the CRL3 ubiquitination machinery into SA-induced NPR1 condensates is an essential function of NPR1 in mediating protein homeostasis and cell survival.

Chromatoid bodies (CBs) are germ cell specific RNP granules localized in the cytoplasm of spermatids. CB forms as spermatogenesis switches between the meiotic and post-meiotic phases and is involved in the regulation of the haploid male germ cell's exceptionally diverse transcriptome.

Condensate (IMC or intramidochondrial cement) is found in vertebrate male germ cells, where it acts a glue that teathers clusters of mitochondria. Several functions hjave been identified, includibng piRNA pocessing.|, fusion/fission,

In many animals, maternal cytoplasmic factors called germ plasm regulate gamete production during embryogenesis. Germ plasm is a cytoplasmic determinant  composed mainly of RNAs and proteins and is inherited from the mother to the offspring inside the egg.

A single large granule of nuage, presents in post-meiotic spermatids is called the chromatoid body. Multiple proteins and some mRNAs have been found to localized to the chromatoid body including mouse VASA homolog , tudor-domain containing 1 (TDRD1), tudor-domain containing 6 (TDRD6), and tudor-domain containing 7 (TDRD7) , transition protein 2 (Tnp2), RANBP9, as a known MVH interactor also localizes to it. Its formation is related to the coalescence of intermitochondrial cement granules. In fact, the formation of the chromatoid body is not required for microRNA biogenesis, but might be important for its action on target mRNAs. In mice, the chromatoid body is a structure resembles Gp, TDRD6 plays a role in establishing the body and the localization of piRNA pathway components to this body.

In recent years, molecular identification of the components of these germ cell substances has revealed that the molecular components overlap somewhat and thus germ plasm/granule and nuage have at times been treated as largely equivalent. In primary oocytes of some animals, maternal germ plasm first assembles within an ancient perinuclear oocyte structure known as the Balbiani body and later is found at the oocyte cortex, the posterior pole in some insects or the vegetal pole of some vertebrates. Nuage is the perinuclear granulo-fibrillar electron-dense material that has been identified through histological and ultrastructural examination of oocytes from invertebrates through vertebrates and that is present in various conformations in cells of the male and female gametes.

Germ granules appear as rounded fibrillar aggregates (or nuage) that cluster around nuclei[1]. P-granules, the worm analog of mammalian nuage or germ granules, condense from a pool of diffuse constituents following specific biological cues. A primary constituent of nuage is Ddx4. Typical of non-membrane encapsulated organelles, nuages are generally spherical and dynamically change in number, size, and composition over their lifecycle, appearing first in the juxtanuclear cytoplasm of early spermatocytes, moving toward the base of the flagellum during spermatogenesis before finally dispersing[2].

The AFAP1-AS1 condensate is a biomolecular condensate formed as a result of phase separation of the long non-coding RNA actin filament associated protein 1 antisense RNA 1 (AFAP1-AS1). AFAP1-AS1 condensates regulate RNA alternative splicing by recruiting splicing factors such as serine and arginine rich splicing factor 1 and 3 (SRSF1 and SRSF3).
The CCER1 condensate is a nuclear phase-separated structure important for the histone-to-protamine transition during spermatogenesis, driven by CCER1 protein.
Nuclear bodies are membraneless, RNA-rich organelles in the cell nucleus that concentrate certain nuclear proteins and RNA-protein complexes.
Nuclear bodies are membraneless, RNA-rich organelles in the cell nucleus that concentrate certain nuclear proteins and RNA-protein complexes.
NP bodies are phase separated Pumilio (PUM)  condensates that are formed from inhibiting PUM proteins  by lncRNA NORAD, which prevents aberrant  ultimately mitosis.
Nuclear bodies are membraneless, RNA-rich organelles in the cell nucleus that concentrate certain nuclear proteins and RNA-protein complexes.

nYACS are nuclear condensates which form from the phase separation of YTHDC1 and m6A. The number of nYACs increases in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells and  maintain their survival and  preserve them in an undifferentiated state. At the same time, YTHDC1 protects m64 from RNA degradation.

RBM15 form large condensates within the nucleus. Notably, these condensates exhibit a tendency to co-locatize partially with m6A-modified transcripts, displaying a particular affinity for STYK1 transcripts. The correlation between RBM15 condensates and the advancement of tumors is established through their association with the MAPK pathway in mouse cell lines

The SPRI2 Nuclear Condensate is formed by SHI family transcription factors in the nuclei of Arabidopsis thaliana cells. SHI family transcription factors are essential for interspecific pollen rejection by regulating the expression of target genes such as TBL40 and TBL45.

Vernalization 1 (VRN1) encodes an essential transcriptional repressor for plant vernalization that non-specifically binds DNA and has two B3 DNA-binding domains joined by an intrinsically disordered region. It has been demonstrated that VRN1 generates puncta in plant cell nuclei, pointing to the possibility that it regulates gene expression through LLPS to maintain the vernalized state.
membraneless organelles in nucleus
Extra-nucleolar nuclear domains usually visualized by confocal microscopy and fluorescent antibodies to specific proteins.

Nuclear dicing bodies are nuclear bodies that play an  important role  in miRNAs  control  of gene expression. In plant cells, miRNA processing is a two-step process that takes place inside the nucleus by the enzyme Dicer-like1 (DCL1) and other proteins such as Serrate (SE), a zinc-finger domain protein, and Hyponastic Leaves1, a double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) binding-domain protein (HYL1). It is recently found that dicing bodies are phase separated condensates and their assembly is driven by the phase separation of SE.

MicroRNA (miRNA) production entails the step-wise processing of primary miRNAs (pri-miRNAs) into precursor miRNAs (pre-miRNAs) and miRNA/* duplexes by Dicing complexes containing DCL1, HYL1 and SE, which are localized in nuclear dicing bodies (D-bodies), D-bodies are phase-separated condensates.

Nucleocytoplasmic exchange is mediated by nuclear pore complexes (NPCs). They're massive protein complexes that join the inner and outer nuclear membranes to create channels that span the nuclear envelope. Nucleoporins, which are made up of about 30 different protein components, assemble in many copies to form a complicated cylindrical architecture to the nuclear pores.

The nuclear pore is proposed to be a LLPS stress granules initially condense to form stable cores, possibly with a nascent shell layer, and these cores merge into larger structures through interactions between the shell structures. A stable core assemblies could provide a structural platform for the formation of stress granules, due to the high concentration of IDRs on stress granule components to then rapidly phase-separate a dynamic shell that grows as a result of fusion with other small granules and surface exchange with an increasing pool of untranslating mRNPs. This general principle is also seen in the formation of the nuclear pore, wherein the creation of a high local concentration of FG repeat proteins by the structure of the nuclear pore, allows for a phase transition within the nuclear pore itself, even if the interactions between the FG repeats are relatively weak and non-specific.

Nuclear pore complex (NPC) is primarily a site in the nuclear envelope, which regulates entry and exit of cellular material including proteins and RNA. It comprises at least 30 proteins called nucleoporins . Previously, electron micrographs of the nuclear periphery have revealed that euchromatin tends to localize near NPCs, while heterochromatin lies close to the nuclear periphery and lamina. Not surprisingly, various studies have shown an association between active genes and NPCs. The role of NPCs in genome organization and transcription is well established in yeast; however, its role in higher eukaryotes is just starting to evolve.

The central substructure of the nuclear pore complex (NPC), through which nucleocytoplasmic transport of RNAs, proteins and small molecules occurs. The central transport channel is filled with FG-nucleoporins, which form a selective barrier and provide a series of binding sites for transporter proteins. Characterized S. cerevisiae FG-nucleoporins include Nup159p, Nup145Np, Nup116p, Nup100p, Nsp1p, Nup57p, Nup49p, Nup42p, Nup53p, Nup59p/Asm4p, Nup60p and Nup1. Characterized vertebrate FG-nucleoporins include Nup214, Nup98, Nup62, Nup54, Nup58/45, NLP1, and Nup153.
