definition: Any protein complex that is capable of carrying out some part of the process of cell-cell adhesion.
The purisome is a dynamic metabolic condensate that organizes and coordinates enzymes for de novo purine biosynthesis.

Enzymes within the de novo purine biosynthetic pathway spatially organize into dynamic intracellular assemblies called purinosomes. The formation of purinosomes has been correlated with growth conditions resulting in high purine demand, and therefore, the cellular advantage of complexation has been hypothesized to enhance metabolite flux through the pathway. However, the properties of this cellular structure are unclear. Here, we define the purinosome in a transient expression system as a biomolecular condensate using fluorescence microscopy. We show that purinosomes, as denoted by formylglycinamidine ribonucleotide synthase granules in purine-depleted HeLa cells, are spherical and appear to coalesce when two come into contact, all liquid-like characteristics that are consistent with previously reported condensates. We further explored the biophysical and biochemical means that drive the liquid-liquid phase separation of these structures. We found that the process of enzyme condensation into purinosomes is likely driven by the oligomeric state of the pathway enzymes and not a result of intrinsic disorder, the presence of low-complexity domains, the assistance of RNA scaffolds, or changes in intracellular pH.

Pyrenoid is a liquid non-membranous structure in the chloroplast stroma of microalgae. Pyrenoids contain sequestrated Rubisco which is the CO2-fixing enzyme of photosynthesis. Concentration of Rubisco in pyrenoids is believed to increase photosynthesis efficiency.

Pyrenoids are non-membrane-bound, proteinaceous structures that contain a matrix packed with the CO2-fixing enzyme Rubisco. In many species, the matrix is traversed by membrane tubules that are continuous with the photosynthetic thylakoid membranes. Pyrenoids are a central feature of the algal CO2 concentrating mechanism, which supplies Rubisco with a high concentration of its substrate CO2, enabling more efficient carbon capture than that of most land plants. Pyrenoids are found within the chloroplasts of a diverse array of photosynthetic eukaryotes, including nearly all freshwater and marine algae, as well as a group of non-vascular plants.
A non-membrane-bounded organelle found within the chloroplasts of algae and hornworts; responsible for carbon dioxide fixation.

Refractile body condensates undergo dynamic phase separation during the Eimeria tenella's (protozoan parasite infecting chickens) life cycle. They are hypothesized to play roles in nutrient storage, energy metabolism, and immune evasion.
The ORC1 condensate is formed by the host protein ORC1 as a regulatory hub contributing to HIV-1 latency by recruiting repressive epigenetic modifier.

Pre-replication compartments (PRCs) are formed during human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) infection. These condensates are serving as hubs for viral genome replication and transcription. They exhibit liquid-like properties and are essential for efficient viral replication.
viral replication compartments (VRCs) formed by DNA viruses are described as membraneless assemblies or structures within the nucleus of infected cells

The VIR-condensate is a condensate formed within viral replication organelles (VROs) during the replication of positive-strand RNA viruses. It is driven by phase separation of viral replication proteins and incorporates co-opted host proteins to create a dynamic microenvironment that facilitates efficient viral synthesis.

A common viral replication strategy is characterized by the assembly of intracellular compartments that concentrate factors needed for viral replication and simultaneously conceal the viral genome from host-defense mechanisms. Recently, various membrane-less virus-induced compartments and cellular organelles have been shown to represent biomolecular condensates (BMCs) that assemble through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). In the present work, we analyze biophysical properties of intranuclear replication compartments (RCs) induced during human adenovirus (HAdV) infection. The viral ssDNA-binding protein (DBP) is a major component of RCs that contains intrinsically disordered and low complexity proline-rich regions, features shared with proteins that drive phase transitions. Using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and time-lapse studies in living HAdV-infected cells, we show that DBP-positive RCs display properties of liquid BMCs, which can fuse and divide, and eventually form an intranuclear mesh with less fluid-like features.

The transcription terminator Rho phase separates in the bacterium Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron under nutrient starvation. Rho condensation required for transcription termination of some genes (PMID: 36927025).
A macromolecular complex that contains both RNA and protein molecules.

Alexander disease (AxD) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder caused by dominant gain-of-function mutations in the gene encoding glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), an intermediate filament protein expressed almost exclusively in astrocytes.The defining pathological feature of AxD is the abundant presence in astrocytes of GFAP-containing protein aggregates, called Rosenthal fibers (RFs), especially in the subpial, perivascular, and subventricular regions of the central nervous system.
Nuclear bodies are membraneless, RNA-rich organelles in the cell nucleus that concentrate certain nuclear proteins and RNA-protein complexes.

Eukaryotic cells are inhomogeneously crowded with biological macromolecules (proteins and nucleic acids) and often contain numerous cellular bodies, including proteinaceous membrane-less organelles (PMLOs), They are formed as a result of highly regulated and reversible liquid-liquid demixing phase separation and represent condensed liquid droplets, which are invariantly enriched in intrinsically disordered proteins. Sam68 nuclear bodies (SNBs) is a kind of these bodies located in Nucleus, Its component of Nucleic acids or RNPs are Chloroplast-specific mRNAs Long non-coding RNA, and it is related to mRNAs trafficking through the nucleus.

Sam68 (Src-associated in mitosis 68 kDa) is the prototypic member of the STAR (Signal Transduction and Activation of RNA) family of RNA-binding proteins, which regulate splicing in response to signalling cascades. Nuclear Sam68 protein is concentrated within subnuclear organelles called SLM/Sam68 Nuclear Bodies (SNBs), which also contain some other splicing regulators, signalling components and nucleic acids.

FXR-driven condensates formed by FXR proteins in coordination with the SARS-CoV-2 protein Nsp3. These condensates play a role in clustering viral replication organelles and recruiting the machinery necessary for efficient replication.

The SARS CoV-2's nucleocapsid (N) protein binds the virus's RNA genome to and packages to forma membrane-bound virion. In cells, N forms condensates which recruits the stress granule protein G3BP1. Phase separation of the SARS-CoV-2 N protein might play a dual role in suppressing the host immune response which involves G3BP1 assembly to stress granules and packaging genomic RNA during virion formation.

SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein (N-protein) undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) with viral RNA. N-protein condenses with specific RNA genomic elements under physiological buffer conditions and condensation is enhanced at human body temperatures (33°C and 37°C) and reduced at room temperature (22°C). RNA sequence and structure in specific genomic regions regulate N-protein condensation while other genomic regions promote condensate dissolution, potentially preventing aggregation of the large genome. N protein/RNA LLPS may be essential for SARS-CoV-2 viral assembly.
Sec bodies are reversible non-membrane bound stress assemblies that incorporate components of the ER exit sites. These assemblies form in Drosophila S2 cells in response to amino-acid starvation.

Upon the stress of amino acid starvation in Krebs Ringer bicarbonate buffer (KRB), the ER exit sites (ERES) of Drosophila S2 cells are remodeled into large round non-membrane bound phase-separated Sec bodies. They are typically observed by immunofluorescence after staining of endogenous Sec16, Sec23 and expressed Sec24–GFP. Importantly, Sec bodies are very quickly resolved upon stress relief (addition of growth medium). Finally, they appear to protect the components of the ERES from degradation and they help cells to survive under conditions of amino acid shortage.
Signaling clusters are protein assemblies which form at the membrane surfaces. Signaling clusters are crucial for the regulation of cell signaling.

One of the most actively studied areas in which spatial heterogeneity is emerging as a key factor is signal transduction at the cell membrane. In addition to imposing a quasi-two-dimensional geometry, the membrane plays host to a large diversity of cellular components, and interactions among these components give rise to a complex spatial organization. A central theme of recent work in this field is the prevalence and role of membrane clusters, groups of colocalized molecules that often participate in the detection of external signals and subsequently drive responses within the cell.

Membrane clusters is groups of colocalized molecules that often participate in the detection of external signals and subsequently drive responses within the cell[1]. Clustering of proteins into micrometer-sized structures at membranes is observed in many signaling pathways. Most models of clustering are specific to particular systems, and relationships between physical properties of the clusters and their molecular components are not well understood. Polymerization and concomitant phase separation is a general mechanism to create membrane clusters[2]. Besides, T cell receptors microclusters are a substructure within the T cell immunological synapse, which have now emerged as the primary functional signaling units[3].

BMP2K(BMP-2-inducible protein kinase), a key regulator of bone differentiation, forms cytoplasmic condensates (even though, it is described to have a nuclear localization signal (NLS)). Under hyperosmotic stress, these condensates increase in number while their average size decreases.
DDR1 condensate in vascular smooth muscle cells counteracts the stiffness/collagen-induced YAP-Hippo pathway.
EML4-ALK fusion oncoprotein common to human cancers forms cytoplasmic biomoelcular condensates, which participate in MAPK signalling
Insulin/IGF-1 signalosomes are condensates functioning as organizing center for insulin/IGF-1 signaling. IRS-1 with aberrant liquid-like properties are implicated in metabolic diseases.

Mechanistically, hCINAP interacts with and prevents NEDD4 from forming cytoplasmic condensates that compartmentalize YAP1 and its kinase NLK, facilitating YAP1 phosphorylation at Ser128 and promoting YAP1 activation.

The condensates formed by PARP5A and RNF146 are dynamic molecular assemblies with liquid-like properties. They are involved in regulating cellular mechanisms, including restraining necroptosis by organizing specific signaling pathways.

PGAM5-MAVS condensates are biomolecular condensates formed through LLPS in cardiomyocytes under stress conditions.

These condensates function as scaffolds for NLRP3 inflammasome activation, thereby playing a role in inflammatory responses and myocardial injury.
Hpo kinase complexes undergo clustering and phase separation
The TBC1D2B condensate forms through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) upon autophagy induction, transitioning from a dilute state to spherical gel-like compartments with high protein mobility.

SINT speckles are membraneless cytosolic speckles formed in response to cellular stress. SINT speckles partially colocalize with active TBK1, and TBK1 phosphorylation is reduced when SINTBAD and the SINT speckle component AZI2 are deleted. The acetyltransferase KAT2A (GCN5) regulates the dynamic production of SINT speckles, which is inhibited by heat shock protein-mediated chaperone action. The autophagy-initiating kinases ULK1/2 also suppress SINT speckle formation, and knocking these kinases out prevented focal TBK1 phosphorylation in a pathway-specific manner.

cellular stress leads to the incorporation of the adaptor protein SINTBAD (TBKBP1) into membraneless, cytosolic speckles. Determination of the interactome identified >100 proteins forming constitutive and stress-inducible members of an MLO that we termed SINT-speckles. SINT-speckles partially colocalize with activated TBK1, and deletion of SINTBAD and the SINT-speckle component AZI2 leads to impaired TBK1 phosphorylation. Dynamic formation of SINT-speckles is positively controlled by the acetyltransferase KAT2A (GCN5) and antagonized by heat shock protein-mediated chaperone activity.

siRNA bodies are specific cytoplasmic foci in Arabidopsis thaliana which contain accumulated AGO7, SGS3 and RDR6.  siRNA ibodies are distinct from P-bodies, but become positive to stress granule markers under stress induced translational repression, implying that siRNA bodies may store stalled mRNAs.

siRNA bodies are RNA granules associated with the synthesis of tasiRNA and the amplification of the RNA silencing signal. Many plant viruses interfere with siRNA body functions in order to suppress their contribution to siRNA production. Upon stress-induced translational repression, siRNA bodies become positive for stress-granules markers, suggesting that these bodies may accumulate stalled mRNAs.
The slit diaphragm condensates are described to form through the process of liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), driven by multivalent interactions among key scaffold proteins at the diaphragm.

Slit diaphragm is a specialized adhesion junction between the opposing podocytes, establishing the final filtration barrier to urinary protein loss. At the cytoplasmic insertion site of each slit diaphragm there is an electron-dense and protein-rich cellular compartment that is essential for slit diaphragm integrity and signal transduction. Mutations in genes that encode components of this membrane-less compartment have been associated with glomerular diseases. We demonstrated that MAGI2, a unique MAGUK family scaffold protein at slit diaphragm, can autonomously undergo liquid-liquid phase separation. Multivalent interactions among the MAGI2-Dendrin-CD2AP complex drive the formation of the highly dense slit diaphragm condensates at physiologic conditions.

Given that Rpp20 is found both in the cytoplasm and the nucleus, it is possible that Rpp20 has additional functions in the cytoplasm. Indeed, Rpp20 has been found to be a stress-responsive protein in the cytoplasm that is redistributed into cytoplasmic SMN granules in adverse conditions.

The survival of motor neuron protein (SMN) is an ubiquitously expressed 40 kDa protein found in the cytoplasm, the nucleoplasm and nuclear Cajal bodies.Reduced levels of SMN cause spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), an autosomal recessive disease characterized by degeneration of motor neurons in the spinal cord. SMN functions as a core complex with at least eight other proteins: SIP-1 or gemin2, dp103 (gemin3, a putative RNA helicase), gemin4, which binds SMN indirectly through gemin3, and gemins 5, 6, 7, 8 and unrip. This SMN complex appears to be involved in the assembly and methylation of U snRNPs in the cytoplasm and their subsequent transport into the nucleus.
conserved spider silk spidroin protein

The paper shows that human EB1 forms molecular condensates with TIP150 and MCAK through liquid–liquid phase separation to compartmentalize the kinetochore–microtubule plus-end machinery, ensuring accurate kinetochore–microtubule interactions during chromosome segregation in mitosis. The give evidence in vitro and in vivo in hela cells and also show formation of these condensates upon microinjection in drosophila syncitial embryos.
+TIP body is the condensate concentrating proteins at the growing tip of the microtubule.
The chromosomal passenger protein birc5b localizes to the tips of astral microtubules and organizes microfilaments and germ plasm in the zebrafish embryo.
EBF1 condensates are phase-separated structures formed by the transcription factor EBF1, driven by its intrinsically disordered region (IDR) containing regularly spaced tyrosines.

The GAS2L3 condensate is a biomolecular condensate formed as a result of growth arrest-specific 2 like 3 (GAS2L3) protein phase separation driven by the intrinsically disordered region (IDR) of GAS2L3. GAS2L3 condensates scaffolds CHMP4B at the cell midbody during cytokinesis to accelerate cell division and promote tumor growth.

Spindle assembly which is an important step during mitosis requires microtubule polymerization. BuGZ phase separates and associates with microtubules and tubulin and this process leads to the assembly of spindle matrix.

The spindle is an important structure when cells divide. Phase separation promotes the concentration of molecules into the droplets, thereby promoting biochemical reactions. Some protein mixtures undergo a phase change to form droplets that concentrate actin to promote F-actin assembly in vitro. In addition, studies have shown that the phase transition of spindle regulatory protein BuGZ concentrates tubulin and promotes MT polymerizationbinds to tubulin and promotes spindle assembly.

The spindle is an important structure when cells divide. Phase separation promotes the concentration of molecules into the droplets, thereby promoting biochemical reactions. Some protein mixtures undergo a phase change to form droplets that concentrate actin to promote F-actin assembly in vitro. In addition, studies have shown that the phase transition of spindle regulatory protein BuGZ concentrates tubulin and promotes MT polymerizationbinds to tubulin and promotes spindle assembly
A proteinaceous, nuclear-derived structure that embeds the microtubule spindle apparatus from pole to pole in a microtubule-independent manner during mitosis.

Pre-mRNA splicing is catalyzed by the spliceosome, a multimegadalton ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex comprised of five snRNPs and numerous proteins. Intricate RNA-RNA and RNP networks, which serve to align the reactive groups of the pre-mRNA for catalysis, are formed and repeatedly rearranged during spliceosome assembly and catalysis. Both the conformation and composition of the spliceosome are highly dynamic, affording the splicing machinery its accuracy and flexibility, and these remarkable dynamics are largely conserved between yeast and metazoans.
Sponge bodies are sub-cellular structures in the cytoplasm of oocyte and nurse cell in Drosophila ovaries. Sponge bodies are crucial in transcription regulation

Sponge bodies are 500-3,000 nm structures which are embedded in an electron dense matrix that is free of ribosomes. Btz, Tral, Cup, eIF4E, Me31B, Yps, Gus, Dcp1/2, Sqd, BicC, Hrb27C, Bru were identified in sponge bodies with Exu-GFP indicating that these structures have a role in post-transcriptional gene regulation. Since sponge bodies are typical proteinaceous membrane-less organelles, liquidâliquid phase separation is shown in the formation and disassembly of sponge bodies.

SPOP/DAXX bodies are nuclear bodies which form by phase separation of SPOP/DAXX in the nucleus. SPOP and DAXX are suggested to interact with each other and together they colocalize at distinct spots in the nucleus and form  a different, largely spherical type of nuclear body distinct from nuclear speckles, PML bodies, nucleoli, and Cajal bodies; named SPOP/DAXX bodies. Mutations which disrupt the interaction between SPOP and DAXX localizes SPOP to nuclear speckles and DAXX to the PML bodies.
STD1 bodies are  nuclear puncta in yeast which controls the response to energy depletion by SNF1.

Biomolecular condensates are micron-scale compartments in eukaryotic cells that operate to concentrate proteins and nucleic acids but lack surrounding membranes. RNA metabolism, ribosome biogenesis, the DNA damage response, and signal transmission are all affected by these condensates. Recent research has discovered that multivalent macromolecular interactions promote liquid-liquid phase separation, which is a fundamental organizing principle for biomolecular condensates.

In DNA virus-infected cells, excessively produced 2′3′-cGAMP triggers the phase-separation of ER-associated STING to form a biocondensate with organized membranous structures, the STING phase-separator, to separate STING-TBK1 from IRF3 and prevent innate immunity from overactivation. The STING phase-separator may act like a ‘STING-TBK1-cGAMP sponge’, and probably bypasses the requirement for intracellular 2′3′-cGAMP-specific hydrolase.

DHX9 Granules are a subtype of stress granules (SGs). DHX9 Granules are biomolecular condensates composed of RNA and proteins that form in response to RNA damage induced by UVB or UVC irradiation. They contain a substantial amount of damaged RNA, including intronic sequences. The primary protein constituent of these granules is DHX9, which facilitates their formation through binding to the damaged RNA. These condensates play a critical role in sequestering damaged RNA to prevent its translation and aid in cellular recovery processes.
Cytoplasmic condensates formed under stress, distinct from stress granules (SGs), promote internal ribosome entry site (IRES)-mediated translation.
During Dictyostelium discoideum development, HSP48 is  strongly induced. It is discovered that HSP48 forms a biomolecular condensate and that polyphosphate is required to keep it stable.

The PCBP2 condensate is a biomolecular condensate formed as a result of phase separation of poly(C)-binding protein 2 (PCBP2). PCBP2 condensates sequester mitochondrial and mRNA-binding proteins, leading to the outside impairment of mitochondrial morphology and function, and BACE1 mRNA decay relative to amyloid deposition. Mitochondrial proteins sequestered by PCBP2 are not found in reported processing bodies (PB) or stress granules (SG).
Biomolecular condensate of RPSA, amplified by Streptococcus suis  Enolase.

SCOTIN/SHISA-5 (with the help of its intrinsically disordered region (IDR)) forms biomolecular condensates along the membrane of endoplasmic reticulum (ER). It was showen to sequester Sec31/13 and impede ER-to-Golgi vesicle transport.

Trypanosoma brucei

Stress granules in the unicellular protest and parasite Trypanosoma brucei form under heat shock and puromycin treatment, upon polysome disassembly, at the periphery of the cell and are distinct from P-bodies.

YBX1 is proposed to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form condensates in vitro and in cells . YBX1 condensates recruit microRNAs (such as miR-223) in vitro and into exosomes secreted by cultured cells.

Stress granules are assemblies of untranslating messenger ribonucleoproteins (mRNPs) that form from mRNAs stalled in translation initiation, which form through interactions between mRNA-binding proteins that link together populations of mRNPs. Stress granules are a kind of conserved cytoplasmic mRNP and represent an active liquid wherein energy input maintains their dynamic state, its formation modulates the stress response and signaling pathways. Besides, stress granules facilitate the establishment of an antiviral state by limiting viral protein accumulation and regulating signalling cascades that affect virus replication and immune responses.

Stress granules are large cytoplasmic foci that are nucleated by the aggregation of untranslated messenger ribonucleoproteins (mRNPs), which accumulate as a result of stress-induced translation arrest. These transient, non-membrane-bound organelles are hubs that orchestrate stress responses and cell fate. Stress granule formation can interfere with viral replication because all viruses require the host translation machinery to synthesize viral proteins[1]. Their assembly is triggered by a variety of environmental stresses including heat shock, oxidative stress, hyperosmolarity, viral infection, and UV irradiation, but not X-irradiation or DNA-DNA-damaging agents. Their mRNA composition is selective—they contain transcripts encoding housekeeping genes but exclude those encoding stress-induced genes such as HSP70. Stress granules are found in both cultured cell lines and intact tissues[2].
A dense aggregation in the cytosol composed of proteins and RNAs that appear when the cell is under stress.

When yeast is under stress, Sup35 creates protective gels through pH-controlled liquid-like phase separation and gelation. Phase separation in this instance is facilitated by the N-terminal prion domain and controlled by the nearby pH sensor domain. The Sup35 translation factor is through this process protected from stress-related damage by phase separation, which aids in yeast survival.

In human cell models, stressors could promote the abnormal phase separation of α-synuclein, leading to the formation of solid-like, pathological aggregates. This process is linked to cellular stress, including the unfolded protein response, and is considered a key step preceding aggregation in neurodegenerative diseases. In C. elegans models expressing human α-synuclein, the environmental pollutant PHCZ accelerates the formation of α-synuclein condensates and reduces their fluidity, promoting a pathological solid-like state.

Abnormal deposition of α-synuclein in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) of the brain in mice causing damage to dopaminergic neurons. This pathological aggregation of α-synuclein is linked to neuronal dysfunction and the impairment of fear memory.

Synaptic vesicles at a living central synapse are organized as a distinct liquid phase maintained by interactions via the intrinsically disordered region of synapsin. Synapsin condensates recruit α-synuclein, and while enriched into these synapsin condensates, α-synuclein still maintains its high mobility. The presence of synaptic vesicles (SVs) enhances the rate of synapsin/α-synuclein condensation, suggesting that SVs act as catalyzers for the formation of synapsin condensates. At physiological salt and protein concentrations, α-synuclein alone is not able to cluster isolated SVs. Excess of α-synuclein disrupts the kinetics of synapsin/SV condensate formation.
T-cell signalling is a dynamic process involving a large number of membrane and cytosolic proteins, involved in signal transduction.

A multi-protein complex containing at least the T-cell receptor complex and the LAT (linker for activation of T cells) scaffold protein. Also contains a variety of signaling proteins including co-receptors, kinases, phosphatases and adaptors such as CD8. Connects events on the plasma membrane to distal signaling cascades to ultimately modulate T cell biology.

RNase mitochondrial RNA processing (MRP) is an endoribonuclease that degrades particular mRNAs important in cell cycle regulation. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae RMP is named Tam body, which is a specialized processing body that is temporally and asymmetrically regulated during the cell cycle, they are involved in the degradation of cell cycle regulated and daughter cell localized transcripts.

Specialized structures in S.cerevisiae referred to as TAM bodies (temporal asymmetric MRP bodies) are observed exclusively during mitosis. These structures contain Xrn1p but also RNase mitochondrial RNA processing (MRP), which is an essential and highly conserved RNP complex found in eukaryotes. RNase MRP is involved in ribosome biogenesis by processing ribosomal RNA transcripts to produce primers for mitochondrial DNA replication and it cleaves S.cerevisiae B-type cyclin (CLB2) mRNA. Colocalization of Xrn1p with RNase MRP to GW/P body-like structures suggests these ribonucleases regulate mitosis by degrading mRNAs encoding cell cycle regulators.

Inclusion bodies are insoluble aggregates of misfolded proteins inside the cell. A common pathogenic event in a range of neurodegenerative illnesses is aggregated proteins from the cytoplasm of nerve cells and glia. Alzheimer's disease, liquid Tau droplets insoluble Tau aggregates over time.

Inclusion bodies are insoluble aggregates of misfolded proteins inside the cell. A common pathogenic event in a range of neurodegenerative illnesses is aggregated proteins from the cytoplasm of nerve cells and glia. Alzheimer's disease, liquid Tau droplets insoluble Tau aggregates over time.

Tau, a microtubule-associated neuronal IDP, is involved in microtubule stabilization, regulates axonal outgrowth and transport in neurons. Tau can accomplish some of its cellular activities via LLPS. However, liquid-to-solid transition resulting in the abnormal aggregation of tau is associated with neurodegenerative diseases. Tau condensates play a role for neurodegenerative diseases by transitioning into aggregated forms of tau. Tau condensates are involved in microtubule binding, nucleation, and bundling. Tau condensates are interacting with RNA molecules, which could impact RNA homeostasis and transcription.

The TIS granule is a filamentous condensate that shares a large surface area with the rough endoplasmic reticulum and is involved in membrane protein trafficking. Large unstructured areas in mRNAs which exist in Tis granules have a high proclivity for forming a ubiquitous intermolecular interaction network, which act as the condensate skeleton. Because the underlying RNA network precludes full fusing of spherical liquid-like condensates, Tis granule is an irregularly shaped membrane-less organelles. The large surface area created by the condensate surface and the interface with other organelles could enhance interactions.
The BRD4 condensate is a type of biomolecular transcriptional condensate formed by the coactivator BRD4. Its formation is facilitated by the YTHDC1/m6A-eRNA (enhancer RNA).

The condensates formed by the cBAF (canonical BAF) complex, which are influenced by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of ARID1A/B. These condensates are playing a role in chromatin targeting and remodeling and gene regulation.
CEBPZ protein undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation. Affecting its phase separation seems to alleviate signs of liver fibrosis.

The c-Maf condensate is a biomolecular condensate formed as a result of phase separation of the transcription factor c-Maf. Alanine‐rich intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in c‐Maf drive hydrophobic interactions, enabling phase separation. c‐Maf recruits RNA Polymerase II via phase separation to establish transcriptional condensates that upregulate Mtbp transcription.
eukaryotic topoisomerase ii is a condensate formed by eukaryotic Type IIA topoisomerases (topo IIs) (enzymes that modulate chromosome supercoiling) at physiological enzyme concentrations

Biomolecular condensates of the EWS-FLI1 fusion oncoprotein (part of the FUS/EWS/TAF15 (FET) family), is one of the most frequently involved fusion genes in Ewing sarcoma. These condensates are associated with pathogenecity in Ewing sarcoma.

The EWSR1 condensate is a biomolecular condensate that forms as a result of phase separation of EWS RNA-binding protein 1 (EWSR1), driven by its intrinsically disordered N‚Äêterminal and C‚Äêterminal domains, particularly C-terminal RNA recognition motifs. These condensates act as regulatory hubs by sequestering interacting factors (e.g., the m‚Å∂A reader YTHDF2), thereby altering RNA processing and stability.
IRF3/IRF7 condensate stimulating IFN-I transcription.
after cell exposure to IFNγ, KAT8 first binds to amino acids 21–42 in the N-terminal DNA-binding domain (DBD) of induced IRF1, and the IDRs of the two proteins promote KAT8–IRF1 condensate formation
Dynamic nuclear condensates involved in transcriptional regulation during myogenesis.

The METTL14 condensate is formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of the methyltransferase-like 14 (METTL14) protein, mediated by phosphorylation. The condensate is thought to participate in the process of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of mRNA. The condensate is studied in the context of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, during which, the condensate could be targeted to prevent condensate formation and preventing the modification of mRNA.
The Nur77 condensate is  formed through the liquid-liquid phase separation of the nuclear receptor Nur77 on ubiquitinated mitochondria.

Through interactions with activators, RNA polymerase (Pol) II's C-terminal disordered region (CTD) produces clusters or hubs at active genes. CTD droplets are dispersed by CTD phosphorylation and are capable of incorporating intact Pol II.

SGF29 forms liquid-like nuclear condensates during senescence that localize at senescence-associated gene loci, recruiting transcriptional machinery. These condensates interact with chromatin and nascent RNA, regulating senescence-linked transcriptional programs and reinforcing cellular aging through activation of senescence genes.

The TFAP2β condensate is formed through phase separation of transcription factor AP-2 beta (TFAP2β). TFAP2β undergoes condensation in the nucleus to bind the zinc finger protein 131 (ZNF131) promoter.

Transcription bodies of zebrafish embryo are enriched for initiating and elongating forms of RNA polymerase II as well as pioneer transcription factors such as Nanog and Sox19B. They are formed at the mir430 genomic locus and are enriched for miR430 micro RNA.

Transcription Elongation Condensate form at active gene loci during pause release and elongation. They re enriched with active Pol II (Ser5P, Ser2P) and co-localize with nascent RNA and DNA, especially at paused genes. These condensates are important for regulating transcriptional pause release and elongation.

Transcriptional condensates are bimolecular condensates which form by phase separation of transcription factors, mediator cofactors and numerous nucleic-acid binding proteins at enhancer sites of gene loci, promoting bimolecular interactions which are necessary for gene expression.

RNA Polymerase transition from a dispersed to clusters  as E.coli cells enter log phase in nutrient-rich media. These transcription condensates concentrate RNAP and transcription factors (such as NusA).

Release of paused RNA polymerase II (Pol II) requires incorporation of the positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb) into the super elongation complex (SEC), thus resulting in rapid yet synchronous transcriptional activation. However, the mechanism underlying dynamic transition of P-TEFb from inactive to active state remains unclear. Here, we found that the SEC components are able to compartmentalize and concentrate P-TEFb via liquid-liquid phase separation from the soluble inactive HEXIM1 containing the P-TEFb complex. Specifically, ENL or its intrinsically disordered region is sufficient to initiate the liquid droplet formation of SEC. AFF4 functions together with ENL in fluidizing SEC droplets. SEC droplets are fast and dynamically formed upon serum exposure and required for rapid transcriptional induction.

The transcription factors (TFs) regulating cell identity contain prion-like domains (PrLDs) that enable liquid-liquid demixing and the formation of phase-separated condensates. The assembly of the transcription machinery at genomic sites occurs through liquid-liquid phase separation, leading to the formation of transcriptional condensates. Repeat expansions in intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of transcription factors (TFs) alter the phase separation capacity of those TFs, and their capacity to form transcriptional condensates with components of the transcription machinery.

A nuclear DNA-directed RNA polymerase complex containing an RNA polymerase II core enzyme as well as additional proteins and transcription factor complexes, that are capable of promoter recognition and transcription initiation from an RNA polymerase II promoter in vivo. These additional components may include general transcription factor complexes TFIIA, TFIID, TFIIE, TFIIF, or TFIIH, as well as Mediator, SWI/SNF, GCN5, or SRBs and confer the ability to recognize promoters.
U-bodies are specific cytoplasmic RNA granules which are sites for for snRNP assembly aided by U-snRNPs and SMN.

U body is uridine-rich small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (U snRNPs). Drosophila SMN complex proteins Gemin2, Gemin3, and Gemin5 are components of U bodies. And U bodies have recently been described in human cells as discrete 200-400 nm nonmembranous cytoplasmic microdomains containing uridine-rich small nuclear ribonucleoproteins U1, U2, U4/U6 and U5 (U snRNPs). U bodies may be involved in snRNP and mRNA assembly and/or transport. U snRNPs are assembled in the cytoplasm into U bodies, which also contain essential snRNP (splicesome) assembly factors, suggesting that U bodies are sites for assembly or storage of snRNPs before being imported into the nucleus.

Ubiquilins (UBQLNs) are multifunctional proteins that interact with a variety of components of the cell's protein quality control (PQC) machinery. UBQLN mutations are most frequently connected to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and other neurodegenerative diseases. Studies have shown that UBQLN proteins undergo phase separation and form condensates and pathogenic aggregates.

All brain-expressed ubiquilins exhibit self-association behavior manifesting as condensates, they follow distinct courses of phase-separation and aggregation. The brain-expressed ubiquilins, UBQLNs 1, 2 and 4, are highly homologous proteins that participate in multiple aspects of protein homeostasis and are implicated in neurodegenerative diseases. UBQLN2 is intrinsically prone to self-assemble into higher-order complexes, including liquid-like droplets and amyloid aggregates. UBQLN2 self-assembly and solubility are reciprocally modulated by the protein's ubiquitin-like and ubiquitin-associated domains. Moreover, a pathogenic UBQLN2 missense mutation impairs droplet dynamics and favors amyloid-like aggregation associated with neurotoxicity.

Inclusions which form from concentrating of the replication machinary of RNA viruses. These inclusions favor enzymatic activities and protect the viral from getting recognized by the cellular receptors.
Herpesvirus forms cytoplasmic Virion Assembly Compartments (cVACs) in the cytoplasm of the infected cell. These compartments exhibit liquid-like properties.
HIV-1 NC, CA, RT, and IN, but not PR, phase separated in vitro and in live cells as HIV-1 biomlecular condensates (BMCs) in live cells.
LANA bodies are dynamic infectious condensates, located in the nucleus of the host cell, containing viral genome and the KSHV protein LANA, which form via phase separation.
GII.4 HuNoV RdRp protein forms condensates in the infected cells for sites for viral replication.

Inclusions which form from concentrating of the replication machinary of RNA viruses. These inclusions favor enzymatic activities and protect the viral from getting recognized by the cellular receptors.
A viral factory located in the cytoplasm of a host cell.

The GCRV viroplasm is a  condensate that organizes viral replication and assembly by concentrating viral proteins and genetic material. It also plays a role in immune evasion by sequestering host antiviral factors, thereby suppressing the host immune response

Viroplasms are cytoplasmic, membraneless structures assembled in rotavirus (RV)-infected cells, which are intricately involved in viral replication. Two virus-encoded, non-structural proteins, NSP2 and NSP5, are the main drivers of viroplasm formation. The structures (as far as is known) and functions of these proteins are described. Recent studies using plasmid-only-based reverse genetics have significantly contributed to elucidation of the crucial roles of these proteins in RV replication. Thus, it has been recognized that viroplasms resemble liquid-like protein-RNA condensates that may be formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of NSP2 and NSP5 at the early stages of infection. Interactions between the RNA chaperone NSP2 and the multivalent, intrinsically disordered protein NSP5 result in their condensation (protein droplet formation), which plays a central role in viroplasm assembly. These droplets may provide a unique molecular environment for the establishment of inter-molecular contacts between the RV (+)ssRNA transcripts, followed by their assortment and equimolar packaging.

A cytoplasmic viral factory that is electron dense due to high levels of viral RNA. Produced by nucleo-cytoplasmic large DNA viruses (NCLDV) like Poxviridae, Asfarviridae and Iridoviridae, and dsRNA viruses like Reoviridae.

WNK bodies are large distinct foci which form in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) as the result of potassium imbalance. WNK body formation is dependent on kidney-specific WNK1 (KS-WNK1), a truncated kinase-defective WNK1 isoform that is strongly expressed in the DCT.

Destruction complex (DC), are condensates comprising scaffold proteins and kinases that regulate β-catenin stability. The centrosome nucleates DC. Enriching GSK3β partitioning on the centrosome controls β-catenin processing and prevents Wnt-driven embryonic stem cell differentiation to mesoderm.

Dishevelled 2 (Dvl2) is hown to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), mediated by its intrinsically disordered region. Dvl2 condensates are important for controlling the assembly of the Wnt receptor signalosome and disruption of the β-catenin destruction complex.
Ubiquitination of Dvl2 through K63 by WWP2 leads to condensate formation, which activate Wnt signaling
LEF1/β-catenin IDR- dependent condensates enhance Wnt signalling and activation of target gene transcription.

Yb-bodies are perinuclear foci in Drosophila ovarian somatic cells, which  are thought to be the site of PIWI interacting RNA (piRNA) synthesis (OSCs). Yb bodies are multivalent condensates that are formed by Yb-Yb homotypic interaction and   interaction with flamenco RNA transcripts, which are the source of transposon-repressing piRNAs.
Female sterile Yb is a primary component of Yb bodies, perinuclear foci considered to be the site of PIWI-interacting RNA (piRNA) biogenesis in Drosophila ovarian somatic cells.
A cytoplasmic part that appears as an electron-dense sphere of around 1.5 micron diameter containing Yb protein found in somatic cells of ovary and testis. There are one to two Yb bodies per cell.

Early germline blastomeres of C elegans contain ZNFX-1, ZSP1, and WAGO-4, which localize to germ granules (P granules). These proteins detach from P granules later in germline development, forming a distinct liquid-like condensate called the Z-granule. Z-granules assemble into organized tri-condensate assemblages with P-granules and Mutator foci in adult germ cells, termed PZM granules.

Z granule formation occurs at a precise time point in germline development. After detaching from nuclei in oocytes as distinct condensates, Z granule constituents mix together with components of the P granule in the one-celled embryo posterior in large primordial granules that also contain PGL-1. Z granule proteins remain mixed with P granule proteins in these large condensates, until the birth of the P4 blastomere, at which point Z granule proteins demix from P granule proteins to create the Z granule compartment. The Z granule remains distinct from, yet directly adjacent to, P granules for the remainder of embryonic and larval development.

Tight junctions are cell-adhesion complexes between neighbouring cells. The membrane-associated scaffolding proteins ZO1 and ZO2 are required for tight junction supra-molecular construction and placement as continuous networks of adhesion strands. Recent research have shown that ZO proteins self-organize membrane-attached compartments by phase separation and identified the multivalent interactions of the conserved PDZ-SH3-GuK supra-domain as the mechanism underlying ZO phase separation.
The polarity protein PATJ protein is recruited to ZO-1 condensates and supports transition of ZO-1 into a condensed surface layer that elongates around the apical interface.

Tight junction associated membrane proteins regulate tight junction assembly in conjunction with zonula occludens protein phase separation, membrane lipids, mechanical force, and polarity signaling proteins. Non-junctional ZO-1 clusters form by phase separation, and direct actin binding of ZO-1 is required for stable incorporation of retrogradely flowing ZO-1 clusters into TJs. ZO proteins self-organize membrane-attached compartments via phase separation. Formation of condensed ZO protein compartments is sufficient to specifically enrich and localize tight-junction proteins, including adhesion receptors, cytoskeletal adapters, and transcription factors.
